name: Condition-of-England Novel and the Edwardian Social Panorama
description: The long realistic novel that takes the whole of a society as its subject — the family, the firm, the town and the state — and measures it against a standard of social justice. Its models are the Victorian industrial novels, its Edwardian examples Galsworthy's The Man of Property (1906) and Forster's Howards End (1910).
historical_development: Inherited from Dickens, Gaskell and Disraeli, the form was renewed at the turn of the century by the new sociology and by the example of the Russian and French realists. It flourished until the war and was then displaced by the inward and experimental novel; its late survivals are the political novels of the thirties.

name: Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind
description: Fiction organised by the movement of a mind rather than by external event: interior monologue, free indirect style, associative rather than chronological order, and a language that attempts to render thought at the speed at which it occurs.
historical_development: The form was prepared by Henry James's late novels and by the French symbolists, theorised by William James ('stream of thought', 1890) and by Bergson, and realised in English by Dorothy Richardson's Pilgrimage (from 1915), James Joyce's Ulysses (1922) and Virginia Woolf's Mrs Dalloway (1925) and To the Lighthouse (1927).

name: Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form
description: Fiction that makes its own construction visible: the collage, the parallel plot, the mythic frame, the parodic catalogue of styles, the book that includes its own theory. Its English summits are Ulysses (1922) and Finnegans Wake (1939), with Wyndham Lewis's The Apes of God (1930) and Djuna Barnes's Nightwood (1936) as its satirical and Gothic counterparts.
historical_development: The experimental novel came from the European avant-garde — Joyce in Trieste and Zurich, Lewis and Pound in London, Stein in Paris — and was distributed through the little magazines and the small presses. Its commercial failure in the 1930s helped turn the next decade back to realism and to documentary.

name: Modernist Long Poem and the Mythical Method
description: The long poem built from fragments, quotation, allusion and a governing myth rather than from narrative: The Waste Land (1922), Pound's Cantos (from 1925), Hart Crane's The Bridge (1930), Eliot's Four Quartets (1943) and David Jones's In Parenthesis (1937).
historical_development: Eliot's essay on Ulysses (1923) named the technique of 'manipulating a continuous parallel between contemporaneity and antiquity' as 'the mythical method'; Pound's editing of The Waste Land made the cut-and-assemble method visible. The form dominated ambitious poetry until the 1950s.

name: Imagist Lyric and the Free-Verse Line
description: The short poem organised around a single hard image or a rapid sequence of images, written in free verse whose unit is the phrase rather than the foot, with no word that does not contribute to the presentation.
historical_development: Codified in 1913 by Pound and Flint, practised by H.D., Aldington, Williams and Amy Lowell, and extended into the longer sequences of H.D.'s Trilogy. It is the technical foundation of most twentieth-century free verse.

name: Georgian Anthology Lyric
description: The short rhymed or blank-verse lyric designed for the anthology: rural subject, conversational tone, regular stanza, a clear single emotion and a shapely close. Named for Edward Marsh's five Georgian Poetry volumes (1912–22).
historical_development: The Georgian anthologies created the first mass market for contemporary verse in England and were the modernists' principal target; the war poetry they contained outlived the series' reputation.

name: Trench Lyric and the War Poem
description: The short poem written from the experience of the First World War: physical detail, colloquial speech, irony, and an ending that refuses consolation. Its central examples are Owen's 'Dulce et Decorum Est' and 'Strange Meeting', Sassoon's 'They' and 'Base Details', Rosenberg's 'Break of Day in the Trenches' and Thomas's 'Rain'.
historical_development: The form was created under censorship between 1915 and 1918, published in small magazines and hand-printed pamphlets (Owen's Poems appeared posthumously in 1920), and canonised by the anthologies of the 1930s and by Fussell's The Great War and Modern Memory (1975).

name: War Memoir and the Autobiographical Testimony
description: The long prose recollection of war service, mixing documentary record with confession and satire: Blunden's Undertones of War (1928), Graves's Good-bye to All That (1929), Sassoon's Memoirs of a Fox-Hunting Man (1928), Aldington's Death of a Hero (1929) and Jones's In Parenthesis (1937).
historical_development: The memoir was written a decade after the war, in the aftermath of the 'war books boom' of 1929–30, and it established the ironic, disenchanted narrative of the war that dominated the century's memory of it.

name: Peasant Play and the Irish Dramatic Movement
description: The one-act or two-act play of Irish rural life, in a heightened dialect prose, built on a single cottage set and a single violent or revelatory situation: Synge's Riders to the Sea (1904) and The Playboy of the Western World (1907), Lady Gregory's The Rising of the Moon (1907) and O'Casey's early Abbey plays.
historical_development: The form was created for the Abbey Theatre by Synge and Lady Gregory out of the folklore of the west and the speech they heard in the cottages of Aran and Galway; it was attacked as a libel on Irish womanhood and Irish virtue, and its riots made it famous.

name: Verse Drama and the Poetic Play
description: Drama written in verse, usually on mythic or historical subjects, intended for the literary theatre rather than the commercial stage: Yeats's Cuchulain plays, Eliot's Murder in the Cathedral (1935) and The Family Reunion (1939), and the choruses of Auden and Isherwood's The Dog Beneath the Skin (1935).
historical_development: The form was the Irish movement's contribution to the European revolt against naturalism and was taken up in the thirties by Eliot as a Christian and by Auden as a political instrument; the Festival of Britain and the postwar verse plays descend from it.

name: Comedy of Manners and the Drawing-Room Stage
description: The three-act drawing-room comedy of wit and marital intrigue, with a symmetrical plot, a single set and dialogue as the principal action: Coward's Private Lives (1930), Maugham's The Circle (1921), Lonsdale's The Last of Mrs Cheyney (1925).
historical_development: The form inherited the Restoration comedy of manners through Wilde and Pinero and was adapted to the interwar West End, where the cinema and the revue forced it toward speed and spectacle; it survived into the 1940s in the comedy of Terence Rattigan.

name: Suffrage Play and the Woman's Drama
description: The short propaganda play written for the women's suffrage campaign: a single scene, a woman protagonist, a debate on the vote, and a demonstration in the last act. Robins's Votes for Women (1907) and Hamilton and St John's How the Vote Was Won (1909) are its central texts.
historical_development: Produced by the Actresses' Franchise League (1908) and the Woman's Theatre season of 1913, the form reached a mass audience in halls and theatres across the country and disappeared with the grant of the vote in 1918 and 1928.

name: Scientific Romance and the Utopian Tale
description: The tale of invention, discovery or future history, built on a single extrapolation and carrying a social argument: Wells's The Time Machine (1895) and A Modern Utopia (1905), Stapledon's Last and First Men (1930), Huxley's Brave New World (1932).
historical_development: The form was created by Wells out of the popular science journalism of the 1890s and the evolutionary theory of the period, and it divided after the First World War into the literary dystopia and the American pulp 'science fiction'.

name: Dystopian Fiction and the Anti-Utopian Satire
description: The imagined society presented as a warning: a managed, hierarchical or technological state whose costs are dramatised through a dissident consciousness. Its central English texts are Huxley's Brave New World (1932), Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949) and, in the same tradition, Forster's 'The Machine Stops' (1909).
historical_development: The dystopia inverted the socialist and Wellsian utopia after the First World War, drawing on Fordism, eugenics, mass advertising and the totalitarian states of the 1930s; it remains the period's most widely read political form.

name: Detective Novel and the Golden Age Mystery
description: The fair-play detective novel: a closed circle of suspects, a murder with a mechanical solution, a sequence of clues and alibis, and an eccentric detective who explains all at the end. Christie's The Murder of Roger Ackroyd (1926) and Sayers's The Nine Tailors (1934) are its technical summits.
historical_development: The form dominated the interwar lending library and was codified by Van Dine's twenty rules (1928) and Knox's Decalogue (1929); the Detection Club (1930) institutionalised it, and its readership crossed every class and educational boundary.

name: Ghost Story and the Modern Weird Tale
description: The short supernatural narrative, usually framed by a document or a testimony, that withholds its apparition until the last pages and withholds its explanation altogether. James's 'Oh, Whistle, and I'll Come to You, My Lad' (1904) and 'Casting the Runes' (1911) established the modern form.
historical_development: The form was carried by the periodical, the Christmas number and the antiquarian scholarship of the late nineteenth century; Lovecraft's 'cosmic' tales gave it an American counter-tradition and a theory in Supernatural Horror in Literature (1927).

name: Modern Short Story and the Magazine Tale
description: The short story of the modern magazine: a single scene or situation, an implied rather than a stated meaning, an ending that opens rather than closes, and a prose stripped of the nineteenth-century narrator's commentary. Joyce's Dubliners (1914) and Hemingway's In Our Time (1925) are its models.
historical_development: The form was shaped by the commercial magazine, by Chekhov's example in translation, and by the little magazines' demand for compression; it became the characteristic form of the Irish, the American and the colonial short story.

name: New Negro Lyric and the Harlem Renaissance Poem
description: The African American poetry of the 1920s, written in blues and jazz rhythms or in the inherited English lyric: Hughes's The Weary Blues (1926), Cullen's Color (1925), McKay's Harlem Shadows (1922), and the folk sermons and work songs collected in James Weldon Johnson's The Book of American Negro Poetry (1922).
historical_development: The form was created by the Great Migration and by the magazines Opportunity and The Crisis; its polemic was Locke's The New Negro (1925) and its quarrel — folk art versus the received poetic tradition — was fought out between Hughes and Cullen.

name: Regional Novel and the American Local-Colour Inheritance
description: The novel of a defined American region, written from inside its speech and customs: Faulkner's Yoknapatawpha, Wolfe's Altamont, Cather's Nebraska, Hurston's Florida, Welty's Mississippi, Steinbeck's Salinas. It inherits the nineteenth-century local-colour sketch and turns it into a tragic form.
historical_development: The form was enabled by the collapse of the agrarian economy, the Great Migration and the modernisation of the 1920s; the Southern Renaissance made it the period's most formally ambitious American mode.

name: Jazz-Age Novel and the Expatriate Romance
description: The novel of the 1920s: money, drink, parties and the impossibility of permanence, told in a plain, understated prose by a narrator who refuses to explain. Fitzgerald's The Great Gatsby (1925) and Hemingway's The Sun Also Rises (1926) are its two central texts.
historical_development: The form was produced by Prohibition, the post-war dollar, the expatriate colony in Paris and the collapse of Victorian sexual morality; its own obituary was written in the decade that followed.

name: Proletarian Novel and the Working-Class Fiction
description: Fiction written from and about the industrial working class, with a collective rather than an individual protagonist and a strike, a lock-out or a migration as its structural crisis: Greenwood's Love on the Dole (1933), Steinbeck's The Grapes of Wrath (1939), Gold's Jews Without Money (1930).
historical_development: The form was created by the Depression and by the Communist and Labour movements of the thirties, by the Federal Writers' Project in America and by the Left Book Club in Britain; it faded after 1939 with the alliance politics of the war.

name: Documentary Prose and the Reportage Book
description: The book of reportage and survey, built from interviews, statistics, transcribed speech and photographs, with the writer as witness rather than inventor: Orwell's The Road to Wigan Pier (1937), Mass Observation's May the Twelfth (1937), Agee and Evans's Let Us Now Praise Famous Men (1941).
historical_development: The form was enabled by cheap photography, the Mass Observation movement (1937), the documentary film movement of Grierson and the Federal Writers' Project; it is the period's principal contribution to non-fictional prose.

name: Critical Essay and the Modern Review
description: The critical essay written for the literary journal and the university: Eliot's 'Tradition and the Individual Talent' (1919) and 'The Metaphysical Poets' (1921), I. A. Richards's practical criticism, William Empson's Seven Types of Ambiguity (1930), F. R. Leavis's Scrutiny (1932–53) and Virginia Woolf's The Common Reader (1925).
historical_development: Criticism became both an academic discipline and a modernist instrument in this period: the Cambridge school created close reading, the Criterion and Scrutiny created the review as an institution, and the essay became the place where the canon was argued.

name: Biography and the Modern Life
description: Biography as a literary form, written with irony, psychological penetration and a novelist's sense of scene: Strachey's Eminent Victorians (1918) and Queen Victoria (1921), Woolf's Orlando (1928), Keynes's Essays in Biography (1933) and the multi-volume lives of the period.
historical_development: The form was revolutionised by Strachey's short, debunking lives, which applied the French method of the 'vie' to the Victorian sage, and by the Freudian account of childhood that made the private life a legitimate subject.

name: Children's Fantasy and the Golden-Age Tale
description: The children's book of the period at its best: the fantasy of the nursery and the other world (Grahame's The Wind in the Willows, 1908; Barrie's Peter and Wendy, 1911; Milne's Winnie-the-Pooh, 1926; Tolkien's The Hobbit, 1937) and the school and family story of the Edwardian nursery.
historical_development: The form was made by the Edwardian cult of childhood and by the illustrated gift book; it is the period's most enduring contribution to popular literature and its most successful export.

name: Nature Essay and the Rural Observation
description: The essay of rural observation, written by a writer who lives in the place described: Edward Thomas's The South Country (1909), W. H. Hudson's A Shepherd's Life (1910), Richard Jefferies's posthumous collections, Nan Shepherd's The Living Mountain (written 1940s) and the countryside columns of the periodical press.
historical_development: The form descends from Gilbert White and Richard Jefferies and was sustained by the walking literature, the nature column and the interwar fear that the motor road and the suburb were destroying the English countryside.

name: Autobiography and the Modern Memoir
description: The autobiography written as a literary work: Sassoon's Sherston trilogy (1928–36), Graves's Good-bye to All That (1929), Yeats's Autobiographies (1926), Edwin Muir's The Story and the Fable (1940) and the childhood memoir of the period.
historical_development: The form was transformed by the war, which made the young man's testimony a public document, and by the Freudian account of childhood, which made the private life the true subject of the memoir.
